thread.title: iRhythm Technologies: Inferior Product Line And Managerial Inefficiency Preclude Profitability - iRhythm Technologies (NASDAQ:IRTC) | Seeking Alpha

author: Andrew Roberts
title: iRhythm Technologies: Inferior Product Line And Managerial Inefficiency Preclude Profitability - iRhythm Technologies (NASDAQ:IRTC) | Seeking Alpha
text:
The market is a pendulum that forever swings between unsustainable optimism (which makes stocks too expensive) and unjustified pessimism (which makes stocks too cheap). The intelligent investor is a realist who sells to optimists and buys from pessimists. - Benjamin Graham, The Intelligent Investor
Investment master Benjamin Graham would undoubtedly attribute the unsustainable revenue growth of iRhythm Technologies ( IRTC ) to market optimists. At current share prices, the 'realist' would sell their holdings before the unsustainable optimism surrounding IRTC dwindles.
Since going public at the end of 2016, shares of IRTC have grown over 200%. This is the result of exhilaration over massive revenue growth which blinds The Street to the inauspicious management and unprofitability that cripple the San Franciscan company. A better term might be fear of missing out.
In an incredible showing of unpunctuality, iRhythm finally launched a telemetric version of their electrocardiographic monitoring device, the Zio XT, last year. The telemetric capable version, the Zio AT, entered a fully penetrated market with over a dozen competitors. Revenues are still completely dependent on Zio XT sales, a device that will be obsolete in the near future.
Shares of iRhythm Technologies are extremely overvalued, with a near-term 35-40% downside risk.
Glory Days iRhythm leveraged the early presence of the Zio XT in the automatic ECG monitoring space to grow sales at a CAGR of nearly 60% over the past five years. This was possible due to the low-tech nature of the ECG monitoring devices the Zio XT competed with. Pictured below is a classic extended Holter monitor, the industry standard for automatic ECG monitoring.
ECG monitoring of cardio patients deemed 'well enough to walk around' is known as ambulatory ECG monitoring. When the Zio XT reached the market, the monitoring options for ambulatory cardiac patients were limited to wire-heavy extended Holter monitors and implantable loop recorders. In recent years, these invasive devices have been largely replaced by the Zio XT, which provides two weeks of continuous ECM without having to remove or replace the device. Patients can sleep, shower, and go about every other aspect of their daily lives without having to remove or adjust the Zio XT monitor. The Zio XT also demonstrated superiority to the aforementioned devices in comparative studies of accurate cardiac event monitoring. All of this said it comes as no surprise that Zio XT sales are approaching $150 million just five years after reaching the market.
iRhythm's ECG monitoring device will have its place in ECG history. The Zio XT progressed the world of ambulatory ECG monitoring and provided cardiac patients with a new level of convenience. Unfortunately, for iRhythm, though, the convenience of the Zio XT exists only in comparison to conventional Holter/implantable devices. Enter telemetry, the bane of the Zio XT.
Twilight Years The introduction of telemetry to the field of ambulatory ECG monitoring marked the beginning of the end for iRhythm. In spite of continuously growing technological development expenses, telemetry is one of many features iRhythm management was inexplicably unable to incorporate into their product line for several years.
In short, telemetry is the automated communication and transmission of data from remote equipment to monitoring locations. Several telemetric ambulatory ECG monitoring devices have been developed in recent years, including the ePatch from BioTelemetry ( BEAT ), the KardiaBand/KardiaMobile/KardiaPro from Alivecor, and the QardioCore from Qardio to name a few. The live transmission features of these devices offer a significant improvement to the extensive processing times of the Zio XT.
Compare this timeline for the Zio XT data transmission process to a real-time transmission from device to doctor and you can begin to understand the fate of iRhythm Technologies.
The pitfalls of the Zio XT are not limited to the delayed transmission times. In arguing the staying power of the Zio XT, management has pointed to the superior monitoring accuracy and lower cost of the device relative to telemetric ECG monitors. The internal studies have shown the Zio XT to be more accurate (albeit marginally) than cherry-picked telemetric devices, but an unbiased comparative study conducted by the American Heart Journal found the Zio XT to be vastly inferior to the Bardy Diagnostics CAM Patch across multiple metrics. In conclusion of the study, electrophysiologist Robert Rho concluded:
The CAM patch identified more arrhythmias than the Zio XT patch...the CAM patch was observed to be easier to attach and remove, more stable, and associated with less skin reaction. Importantly, it was found that the superior signal clarity provided by the CAM patch may result in more informed clinical decisions in over a third of the patients.
The CAM patch also offers users the option to analyze data using their own technicians, a feature not offered by the Zio XT.
Bardy Diagnostics just announced the successful enlisting of the 40,000th CAM patch patient. This is just one of the plethora of devices that are taking would-be Zio XT customers.
An Apple A Day Keeps The Doctors Away (From Zio) iRhythm's biggest competitor is industry giant BioTelemetry , a vastly superior entity with a broad product line of mobile cardiac telemetry devices, event monitors, Holter monitors, and extended Holter monitors. BioTel's ePatch is the most similar product to the Zio XT - it is an extended Holter monitor - with the exception that the ePatch has telemetric capabilities. The market presence of the ePatch is early in its bloom; BioTel acquired the asset from the Danish company DELTA in April of 2016.
Rapid market acceptance of the ePatch will come at the hands of Apple ( AAPL ). In 2017, Apple announced the Apple Heart Study , a breakthrough cardiac study open to the public in which the Apple Watch screens for AF activity. If AF activity is detected by the Apple Watch, the patient is directed to a medical professional to receive an ePatch for more precise monitoring.
The Apple Heart Study has enrolled an estimated 500,000 people in the U.S. There are an estimated 3-6 million people in the U.S. with AF (or 1-2% of the population). So we can conservatively assume that 5,000-10,000 study participants have AF.
Now, a substudy conducted by Apple found that of 226 people whose Apple Watch detected AF activity, 94 (or 41.6%) had AF activity detected by the ePatch afterward. Given this, a reasonable expectation for the number of study participants who will receive an ePatch is 12,000-24,000.
The Apple Heart Study also partners with American Well, a telemedicine company based in Boston with a multi-million physician network. A large percent of these physicians will be introduced to the ePatch with this study, which will colossally extend the market acceptance & penetration of the ePatch.
Brief Financial Discussion The revelry over iRhythm's massive revenue growth should be dampened by the nearly linear growth in net losses. The company continues to post industry-high SG&A expenses which inexplicably eclipse revenues and hinder profitability. Management is destroying value as the company grows.
The trend of losses expanding linearly with revenues will continue as long as iRhythm continues employing a direct payor billing model. Unlike peers, iRhythm assumes reimbursement responsibilities rather than leaving the responsibility to prescribing physicians. This makes the Zio much more attractive to physicians but is a short-sighted means for revenue growth. With this model comes the need for a large customer service/back office team to deal with payment and customer service issues. As sales and customer base grow, so must the customer relations office.
As of September, iRhythm had $81 million in cash & equivalents with $33 million in debt. The company is currently burning over $10 million a quarter, which can be expected to increase given historical trends.
On a positive note, the $35.8 million outstanding Pharmakon debt was refinanced with a $35 million loan from Silicon Valley Bank with a $25 million revolving credit line. This effectively lowered the APR on the outstanding debt from 9.5% to the WSJ Prime Rate + 0.25% (currently 5.75%).
iRhythm also obtained a $6.9 million Standby Letter of Credit from Silicon Valley Bank for the $10 million/year lease entered into for the new company headquarters.
Final Notes In the last year, insiders have been rapidly exercising their derivative grants and selling the underlying stock. A total of 610,000 shares have been converted, 673,000 shares have been sold, and 76,000 shares have been acquired by directors and officers in the last year. This represents a 65% reduction in insider holdings.
iRhythm Technologies is grossly overvalued presently. The entirety of the company's revenues is built on an inferior and outdated device with a broad selection of competitors. Early domination was possible in a market with limited & low-tech options, though management still failed to ever reach profitability. New ECG monitoring devices have demonstrated unequivocal superiority to iRhythm's crown jewel in clinical studies. Moreover, tech-giant Apple partnered with the biggest competitor of iRhythm in selecting an ECG device for the revolutionary Apple Heart Study. It is difficult to imagine a plausible competitive scenario that is less conducive to the future success of iRhythm than the current one.
Presently, shares of iRhythm present a 35-40% downside risk by year end.
